title: Numbers 8:5–22
context: The Levites are cleansed, presented before the whole congregation, and offered to the LORD as a wave offering on Israel’s behalf. The Israelites lay hands on them, the Levites lay hands on the bulls for sin and burnt offerings, and atonement is made for them. God explains that he has taken the Levites in place of Israel’s firstborn, whom he claimed when he struck Egypt’s firstborn (Exodus 13:1–2, 11–15), and gives them to Aaron to serve so that no plague will strike Israel when they approach the sanctuary.

verses.text: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD speaks to Moses about the Levites. Arminian readers note that this begins the formal consecration of the tribe set apart for service. Both traditions agree that the instructions follow the census and assignments of Numbers 3–4.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God himself initiates the Levites’ consecration. Shared ground: the Levites’ role is established by God’s word, not human choice, and the following verses describe their cleansing and presentation.

verses.text: “Take the Levites from among the children of Israel, and cleanse them.
verses.arminianNotes: Moses is to take the Levites from among Israel and cleanse them. Arminian readers see God calling people from among the community for special service. Both traditions agree that cleansing must precede service in the sanctuary.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s choice of the Levites, set apart from the other tribes. Shared ground: those who serve God must first be cleansed, a principle that runs through Scripture.

verses.text: You shall do this to them to cleanse them: sprinkle the water of cleansing on them, let them shave their whole bodies with a razor, let them wash their clothes, and cleanse themselves.
verses.arminianNotes: The Levites are sprinkled with water of cleansing, shave their whole bodies, and wash their clothes. Arminian readers see outward rituals expressing inward readiness for service. Both traditions agree that cleansing prepares them to approach the holy place.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the rituals as signs of purification God requires. The “water of cleansing” is not further explained here. Shared ground: purification precedes service, and the ritual signs point to the need for real cleansing before God.

verses.text: Then let them take a young bull and its meal offering, fine flour mixed with oil; and another young bull you shall take for a sin offering.
verses.arminianNotes: The Levites take a young bull with its meal offering and another bull for a sin offering. Arminian readers see that the Levites, too, need atonement. Both traditions agree that the offerings prepare them for service.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see atonement as necessary before consecration: those set apart to serve are themselves sinners in need of cleansing. Shared ground: the Levites, like the rest of Israel, need the sin offering before they can serve.

verses.text: You shall present the Levites before the Tent of Meeting. You shall assemble the whole congregation of the children of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: The Levites are presented before the Tent of Meeting, and the whole congregation is assembled. Arminian readers see the community’s participation in commissioning its servants. Both traditions agree that the public setting matters.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the assembly as witnesses to God’s appointment of the Levites. Shared ground: the consecration is public, involving the whole people, so that the Levites’ role is recognized by all Israel.

verses.text: You shall present the Levites before the LORD. The children of Israel shall lay their hands on the Levites,
verses.arminianNotes: The Israelites lay their hands on the Levites. Arminian readers see identification: the Levites serve on behalf of the people. Both traditions agree that the laying on of hands expresses representation and transfer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the gesture as signifying that the Levites stand in place of the people, especially the firstborn (8:16–18). Shared ground: the Levites become representatives, and the people own their service.

verses.text: and Aaron shall offer the Levites before the LORD for a wave offering on the behalf of the children of Israel, that it may be theirs to do the service of the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Aaron offers the Levites as a wave offering on behalf of Israel, so that they may serve the LORD. Arminian readers see the Levites given wholly to God. Both traditions agree that the wave offering marks them as dedicated.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Levites as a living offering presented to God. Many readers in both traditions connect this with believers offering themselves (Romans 12:1). Shared ground: the Levites belong to God for service.

verses.text: “The Levites shall lay their hands on the heads of the bulls, and you shall offer the one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering to the LORD, to make atonement for the Levites.
verses.arminianNotes: The Levites lay hands on the bulls, which are offered as sin and burnt offerings to make atonement for them. Arminian readers see personal identification with the sacrifice. Both traditions agree that atonement precedes service.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see substitution in the laying on of hands: the animal stands in the Levites’ place. Shared ground: the Levites need atonement, and both traditions read these offerings as fulfilled in Christ.

verses.text: You shall set the Levites before Aaron and before his sons, and offer them as a wave offering to the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The Levites are set before Aaron and his sons and offered as a wave offering. Arminian readers see their service placed under priestly direction. Both traditions agree that the Levites assist the priests rather than replacing them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the order of service: Levites serve under the priests, assisting rather than replacing them. Shared ground: the consecration places the Levites within God’s ordered structure for the sanctuary.

verses.text: Thus you shall separate the Levites from among the children of Israel, and the Levites shall be mine.
verses.arminianNotes: God separates the Levites from Israel, and they become his. Arminian readers see a calling to belong to God in a special way. Both traditions agree that separation for service is God’s act.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s claim on the Levites as an expression of his sovereign choice. Shared ground: the Levites belong to the LORD, and their separation serves the whole people.

verses.text: “After that, the Levites shall go in to do the service of the Tent of Meeting. You shall cleanse them, and offer them as a wave offering.
verses.arminianNotes: After cleansing and the wave offering, the Levites begin their service in the Tent of Meeting. Arminian readers see the order: consecration first, then work. Both traditions agree that service follows preparation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the sequence as reflecting God’s order: cleansing and dedication precede ministry. Shared ground: those who serve must first be prepared according to God’s word, not by their own initiative.

verses.text: For they are wholly given to me from among the children of Israel; instead of all who open the womb, even the firstborn of all the children of Israel, I have taken them to me.
verses.arminianNotes: God says the Levites are wholly given to him in place of the firstborn. Arminian readers see substitution as God’s gracious provision. Both traditions agree that the Levites represent the firstborn of Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s sovereign right over the firstborn exercised through the Levites, who are “wholly given” to him. Shared ground: the Levites are substitutes for the firstborn, as Numbers 3:12–13 also states.

verses.text: For all the firstborn among the children of Israel are mine, both man and animal. On the day that I struck all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, I sanctified them for myself.
verses.arminianNotes: All Israel’s firstborn belong to God because he sanctified them when he struck Egypt’s firstborn (Exodus 13:2, 15). Arminian readers see God’s claim rooted in redemption. Both traditions agree that the Passover grounds the claim.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see redemption as the basis of God’s ownership: those he saved belong to him. Shared ground: the firstborn were spared at Passover and therefore belong to God, and many in both traditions see a parallel with believers bought at a price (1 Corinthians 6:20).

verses.text: I have taken the Levites instead of all the firstborn among the children of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: God takes the Levites in place of the firstborn. Arminian readers see God’s provision of substitutes. Both traditions agree that the substitution relieves Israel’s families of giving their firstborn sons to sanctuary service.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the substitution as an expression of God’s covenant arrangement, in which one tribe serves on behalf of all. Shared ground: the Levites stand in for the firstborn, fulfilling God’s claim while preserving Israel’s families.

verses.text: I have given the Levites as a gift to Aaron and to his sons from among the children of Israel, to do the service of the children of Israel in the Tent of Meeting, and to make atonement for the children of Israel, so that there will be no plague among the children of Israel when the children of Israel come near to the sanctuary.”
verses.arminianNotes: God gives the Levites to Aaron to serve on Israel’s behalf and make atonement, so no plague strikes when Israel approaches the sanctuary. Arminian readers see protection for the people. Both traditions agree that the Levites guard the holiness of the sanctuary.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Levites as a protective buffer between the people and God’s holiness. Shared ground: their service shields Israel from judgment, and both traditions see a parallel with the protection provided by Christ’s mediation.

verses.text: Moses, and Aaron, and all the congregation of the children of Israel did so to the Levites. According to all that the LORD commanded Moses concerning the Levites, so the children of Israel did to them.
verses.arminianNotes: Moses, Aaron, and the whole congregation do everything as the LORD commanded. Arminian readers see corporate obedience, with every party doing its part. Both traditions agree that the whole people carry out the consecration faithfully.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the repeated formula as emphasizing conformity to God’s word, which the narrative stresses twice in one verse. Shared ground: the consecration is completed according to God’s instructions.

verses.text: The Levites purified themselves from sin, and they washed their clothes; and Aaron offered them for a wave offering before the LORD and Aaron made atonement for them to cleanse them.
verses.arminianNotes: The Levites purify themselves and wash their clothes; Aaron offers them as a wave offering and makes atonement for them. Arminian readers see their active participation in purification. Both traditions agree that atonement is made for them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see both the Levites’ obedience and Aaron’s atoning work as necessary: the Levites purify themselves, but atonement is made for them. Shared ground: purification and atonement precede service.

verses.text: After that, the Levites went in to do their service in the Tent of Meeting before Aaron and before his sons: as the LORD had commanded Moses concerning the Levites, so they did to them.
verses.arminianNotes: The Levites begin their service before Aaron and his sons, as the LORD commanded. Arminian readers see the fruit of consecration in faithful work. Both traditions agree that the consecration is now complete.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Levites’ service as ordered by God and carried out under priestly direction, completing what 8:5 began. Shared ground: the Levites serve as God commanded. Their work begins only now.
